new_statements.rule_in_words: Tenino/Warm Springs is a Sahaptin dialect: each word carries one primary stress (realised as high pitch), and its position is a lexical property of the morphemes, not derived from syllable count or weight (Rude 2006:272, 2012:302-304; Jansen 2010:52-57; Hargus & Beavert 2014 sec. 4.1: 'stress is morpheme inherent in Sahaptin', with stressed suffixes outranking prefixes outranking roots). Hymes 1984 is the only Warm-Springs-specific published statement: p. 229 endorses Jacobs' 1931 sketch as 'roughly valid' for Warm Springs, and p. 235 reports that Warm Springs has dropped the historically stressed vowel of many words and moved the stress to the remaining vowel (pt'xánu, twít'aš, ápx, núkʷt), so Warm Springs stress positions differ lexically from Umatilla/Yakima ones. No source gives a Tenino-specific default-position rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Hymes 1984 says nothing. Jacobs 1931:117 (snippet): Northwest dialects have 'only one syllable accented and no secondary stress', but 'in the Umatilla reservation dialects there may be two, three or four accented syllables to a word'. Rude 2012:302 claims three stress levels for Sahaptin generally with secondary stress considered 'more or less predictable' (Rude 1988: bisyllabic reduplication k'ùsik'úsi 'dog', imperfective past -shàna, habitual -xàna); Hargus & Beavert 2016 find no secondary stress in Yakima. Nothing reported for Warm Springs.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is lexically variable across dialects: Jansen 2010:9 notes the stress of shushaynsh 'steelhead' varies by dialect; Morrison 1990 (per Jansen 2010:275) gives Warm Springs nominaliser -ya with stress on the preceding syllable after polysyllabic C-final nouns vs. stressed -yay elsewhere; unaccented function words such as ku 'and' and pronominal clitics never take stress (Jacobs 1931:117; Hargus & Beavert 2014 sec. 4.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: one accent per phonological word (clitics attach unstressed); citation forms of nouns and verbs. Hymes' data are from Warm Springs (Tenino/Tygh/Wyam speakers on the Warm Springs reservation), 1970s-80s fieldwork; the general rule comes from Umatilla (Rude) and Yakima (Jansen, Hargus & Beavert) descriptions applied to Sahaptin as a whole.
new_statements.identity_note: Hymes 1984 describes 'Warm Springs Sahaptin', the speech of the Warm Springs reservation (Tenino, Tygh Valley, Wyam/Celilo, John Day speakers), which is what Glottolog teni1238 covers (alt. name 'Warm Springs'; Columbia River Sahaptin cluster with Umatilla umat1237). The general stress rule quoted alongside comes from Umatilla (Rude) and Yakima yaki1237 (Jansen; Hargus & Beavert) data stated for Sahaptin as a whole, not from Tenino data.

sources.note: Only Warm-Springs-specific published remark found: p. 229 says Jacobs' 1931 sketch is 'roughly valid' for Warm Springs; p. 235 says many Warm Springs words have lost the stressed vowel that other dialects keep and 'the stress has been shifted to the other vowel of the word' (pt'xanu vs. pat'xanu, twit'as vs. tuwit'as, apx vs. apax, nukwt vs. nakwat). No general placement rule stated; presupposes one lexically stressed vowel per word.

sources.note: Sec. 4.1 Lexical pitch accent: 'Sahaptin morphemes are either underlyingly accented or unaccented'; words surface with one accent; suffix accent wins over root, prefix over root. Yakima/NW data; lists Warm Springs and John Day as Columbia River subdialects.

sources.note: Sec. 2 Stress, pp. 302-304: 'Nez Perce and Sahaptin are syllable timed languages with three levels of stress.. In Sahaptin all lexical morphemes have morpheme inherent stress'; morphemes with inherent stress follow a hierarchy suffix > prefix > root (itxata / patxata / patxatala). Sahaptin data are Umatilla (Columbia River cluster, same cluster as Tenino) with some WS forms; not Tenino-specific.
